metadata.title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
metadata.abstract_summary: Training an LLM to explicitly rank system prompts above user messages above third-party/tool content, and to selectively ignore lower-privileged instructions that conflict with higher-privileged ones, substantially raises robustness to prompt injection and jailbreaks - including attack types never seen during training - while costing little on standard capability benchmarks.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
As the authors state it:

> Today's LLMs are susceptible to prompt injections, jailbreaks, and other attacks that allow adversaries to overwrite a model's original instructions with their own malicious prompts. In this work, we argue that one of the primary vulnerabilities underlying these attacks is that LLMs often consider system prompts (e.g., text from an application developer) to be the same priority as text from untrusted users and third parties. To address this, we propose an instruction hierarchy that explicitly defines how models should behave when instructions of different priorities conflict. We then propose a data generation method to demonstrate this hierarchical instruction following behavior, which teaches LLMs to selectively ignore lower-privileged instructions. We apply this method to GPT-3.5, showing that it drastically increases robustness -- even for attack types not seen during training -- while imposing minimal degradations on standard capabilities.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Synthetic and automatically generated training data demonstrating hierarchical instruction-following (e.g., ignoring an injected instruction found in retrieved content), fine-tuned into GPT-3.5, then evaluated on both in-distribution and held-out attack categories plus standard capability benchmarks to measure the tradeoff.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- Authored and evaluated by OpenAI, primarily on OpenAI's own models and against attack sets partly constructed by the same team - independent, adversarial red-teaming by a separate party is the natural next check the paper's own limitations section points toward.
- The generalization result (robust to attack types unseen during training) is real but measured against categories the authors themselves selected as "unseen," not an open, external bug-bounty-style evaluation.
- Directly relevant to this catalogue's own adapters/openai.py, which currently implements no defense of this kind.
